Warlords Battlecry III is a fantasy real-time strategy game developed by Infinite Interactive and originally released in 2004, later brought to modern digital platforms by Retroism alongside Enlight Software Limited. As the third installment in the Warlords Battlecry series, the game stands out from many other strategy titles of its era by blending traditional RTS mechanics with a surprisingly deep role-playing framework. Instead of focusing purely on base construction and army management, the game introduces a persistent hero character who grows stronger over time and becomes the centerpiece of the entire campaign. This hybrid design creates a unique experience that mixes the large-scale warfare of strategy games with the long-term progression systems commonly found in RPGs.

The game takes place in the fantasy world of Etheria, a land populated by a wide range of civilizations, mystical creatures, and powerful magical forces. The campaign begins with the player assuming the role of a customizable hero traveling aboard a merchant vessel. When a mysterious storm appears around an unknown island, the hero’s curiosity leads them into a series of events that eventually reveal a looming threat to the entire continent. As the story unfolds, players travel across Etheria, confronting rival factions, uncovering ancient secrets, and ultimately facing the apocalyptic force known as Gorgon. While the narrative itself is relatively straightforward, it provides a solid framework that connects the many battles and locations explored throughout the game.

At its foundation, Warlords Battlecry III follows the familiar structure of classic real-time strategy gameplay. Players gather resources, build structures, recruit armies, and command troops in real time against opposing forces. The economy revolves around several key resources including gold, stone, metal, and crystal. Rather than relying heavily on workers gathering materials in the traditional RTS fashion, the game introduces a streamlined system where players capture resource-producing structures scattered across the battlefield. Once secured, these buildings generate resources automatically for the controlling player. This design shifts the focus away from repetitive harvesting and toward strategic map control, encouraging players to expand their territory and contest important locations across the battlefield.

What truly differentiates the game from many other strategy titles is its hero system. At the start of the campaign, players create a hero by choosing a race and class combination from an enormous list of possibilities. The game features sixteen playable races along with numerous class types, allowing for hundreds of potential character builds. Each race and class brings unique abilities, strengths, and weaknesses that shape the hero’s development. As the campaign progresses, the hero gains experience through combat and completed missions, eventually leveling up and unlocking new skills. These abilities can include powerful combat techniques, magical spells, leadership bonuses that enhance nearby units, or economic advantages that improve resource production.

Over time, the hero becomes a powerful presence on the battlefield, often capable of turning the tide of battle when used effectively. Unlike standard RTS units that are easily replaced, the hero represents a persistent character that carries experience, equipment, and abilities from one mission to the next. This sense of continuity gives the campaign a strong feeling of progression and personal investment, as players gradually shape their hero into a legendary warrior, powerful mage, or strategic leader depending on their chosen playstyle.

The game also introduces a unique retinue system that further strengthens the RPG aspects of the experience. Certain units that survive multiple battles alongside the hero can become permanent companions who follow the hero from one mission to another. These retinue units gain experience and improve over time, effectively functioning as loyal allies within the larger army. This system encourages players to protect valuable units and build a small group of elite followers that grow alongside the hero throughout the campaign.

Faction diversity is another major highlight of Warlords Battlecry III. The game includes sixteen distinct races, each with its own architectural style, military units, and strategic strengths. Some races resemble familiar fantasy archetypes such as dwarves, elves, or human knights, while others are far more unusual. Players can command reptilian Ssrathi warriors, insectoid swarms, the necrotic Plaguelords, or other exotic factions that bring radically different playstyles to the battlefield. Each faction has its own technology tree and unit roster, ensuring that strategies vary widely depending on the chosen race. This diversity significantly increases the game’s replay value, as experimenting with different factions often leads to entirely new tactical approaches.

Magic plays a significant role in shaping battles as well. The game features an extensive spell system with a wide variety of magical abilities drawn from multiple schools of magic. Heroes and certain specialized units can unleash devastating spells capable of damaging entire groups of enemies, summoning creatures, or providing powerful buffs to friendly forces. Magic adds an extra layer of tactical depth to combat, allowing players to combine magical effects with traditional military tactics to overwhelm their opponents.

The campaign itself unfolds across a world map that players can explore between battles. Instead of progressing through a strictly linear sequence of missions, players can travel between various cities, villages, and strategic locations across the continent of Etheria. Some locations offer quests or story events, while others provide shops where players can purchase magical items, equipment, or upgrades for their hero. This semi-open campaign structure allows players to approach missions in different orders, creating a sense of exploration and freedom rarely seen in real-time strategy games of the time.

Beyond the campaign, Warlords Battlecry III also offers skirmish battles and multiplayer modes where players can test their strategies against AI or human opponents. These modes allow players to experiment with different factions and hero builds without being tied to the campaign narrative. Given the large number of playable races and character customization options, the game offers substantial replayability even after the main storyline has been completed.

Visually, the game reflects the technological limitations of its early-2000s origins. The graphics rely on detailed sprite artwork rather than modern 3D models, and while the presentation may appear dated compared to contemporary strategy games, the visual design remains functional and easy to read during large battles. Units are clearly distinguishable, and the colorful fantasy environments help bring the world of Etheria to life despite the aging technology.

Ultimately, Warlords Battlecry III remains one of the most distinctive real-time strategy games of its generation. By combining large-scale battlefield strategy with character progression, faction diversity, and a flexible campaign structure, the game offers an experience that feels both expansive and personal. Its blend of RPG mechanics and traditional strategy gameplay creates a level of depth rarely seen in the genre, making it a memorable classic for fans of fantasy strategy games. For players willing to look past its aging visuals, Warlords Battlecry III still stands as a richly rewarding and highly replayable strategy experience.

Rating: 8/10

I don’t think any RTS will ever hit me the way Warlords Battlecry III did. I spent days planning invasions, forming alliances and carefully deciding which territories to defend or liberate. If one of my regions was invaded, I would drop everything to reclaim it. If an ally was struggling, I would march across the map to support them. The campaign map felt alive and every decision truly mattered; I was so sad when my minotaur's allegiance made me an enemy of the empire :(.

But the real magic? The absurd amount of customisation. Dozens of races, countless classes, perks, builds; you could make a demon-summoning necromancer one run, then a dwarven runemaster, then a stealth-focused assassin commander. Every hero was unique. Every playthrough felt different. It was endlessly replayable, and I leaned into that fully.

And the nights online… I’ll never forget them. Hours upon hours with friends, teaming up against brutal CPU armies or turning on each other in chaotic free-for-alls. “One more match” would somehow turn into 3 a.m. more times than I can count.

I’ll always treasure it T_T.

A Real Time Strategy (RTS) game with Role Play (RPG) elements: you create a hero character who follows you through missions, gaining points to put into a skill tree dependant on their race and class. Troops also gain experience and the strongest left alive at the end of each mission can be chosen to join your heroes' retinue. Heroes created in campaign can be used in skirmish mode and multiplayer.

During the campaign, while you start as a particular faction, missions will improve or worsen your reputation with other factions allowing you to chose them for missions once you become allies (or locking them out if they're enemies).

Useful key binds: Game speed can be changed using the - and + keys from "very slow" to "very fast", pausing must be done from the menu though. Pressing "a" before moving will initiate attack move. Spells can be bound to keys by going into the spell book and hovering over the spell with your mouse and pressing the function keys (F1-F12)

Set up to play with compatibility mode (Windows XP Package 2); this will get rid of most of the problems with running the game on newer systems (or at least drastically reduce them)
